title: Watching many connections at once
objective: By the end of this lesson you can use a readiness mechanism to wait on many descriptors from one thread, explain why the older interfaces do not scale, and choose the right one for a given situation.

blocks.text: The previous lesson ended with a problem: a non-blocking descriptor tells you 'nothing yet', and asking repeatedly burns a core. What is missing is a call that sleeps until at least one descriptor in a set becomes ready. That call is the foundation of every high-concurrency server, and there are three generations of it.

blocks.caption: The event loop, independent of which mechanism you use
lines: /* 1. Sleep until at least one descriptor is ready */
/* 2. For each one that is ready, do the work that will not block */
if (it is the listener)  accept a new connection and watch it;
else if (readable)       read what is there and handle it;
else if (writable)       send what is queued for it;
/* One thread. No blocking. No busy loop. Every operation happens
only when it is known that it can proceed. */

blocks.title: The scaling difference is structural, not an optimisation
blocks.text: With select and poll, the kernel is handed the whole list on every call and has to examine all of it — so watching ten thousand mostly idle connections costs work proportional to ten thousand, every time round the loop, to learn that three are ready. epoll is told the set once and reports only what became ready, so the cost tracks the number of active connections rather than the number of open ones. That is the difference between a server that degrades as connections accumulate and one that does not.

blocks.title: select has a hard limit you can exceed silently
blocks.text: Its descriptor set is a fixed-size bit array whose size is a compile-time constant. Using a descriptor number at or above that constant writes past the end of the structure — undefined behaviour, from the C course, in one of its most dangerous forms: it may appear to work. Check the value of FD_SETSIZE on your own system rather than assuming a number, and treat select as unsuitable for any server that may accumulate many descriptors.

blocks.caption: The epoll sequence
lines: ev.events  = EPOLLIN;              /* tell me when it is readable */
int n = epoll_wait(ep, events, 64, -1);   /* -1 = wait indefinitely */

rows: If you read part of it
Not reported again — you must drain it
A connection that silently stalls forever

blocks.title: Edge-triggered mode requires draining, and the bug is silent
blocks.text: If a descriptor is reported readable and you read only some of what arrived, edge-triggered mode will not tell you again until more data arrives. If none does, the remaining bytes sit unread forever and that connection hangs while everything else works. Use level-triggered until you have measured that you need otherwise; when you do use edge-triggered, read in a loop until EAGAIN, on a non-blocking descriptor, without exception.
The rule that makes an event loop work

Nothing in the loop may block. One blocking call — a database query, a file read from a slow disk, a DNS lookup, even a long computation — stops every other connection the loop is serving. This is the discipline the model demands in exchange for handling thousands of connections in one thread, and it is why event-driven runtimes push slow work onto a thread pool rather than doing it inline.

blocks.title: Build the loop
steps: Find your system's select limit: getconf FD_SETSIZE 2>/dev/null || grep -r FD_SETSIZE /usr/include | head -3
Write a server that listens, adds the listener to an epoll set, and loops on epoll_wait
On the listener being readable, accept, set the connection non-blocking, and add it to the set
On a connection being readable, read and echo it back; on read returning 0, remove it and close
Connect several clients at once with nc and confirm one thread serves all of them
Check its CPU use while idle — it should be zero, unlike the busy loop from the previous lesson
Now insert a sleep(5) in the handler and connect two clients — watch the second one wait
Switch one descriptor to edge-triggered, read only 1 byte per event, and watch that connection stall
blocks.expected: One thread serving several clients at zero idle CPU, and then two deliberate failures: a blocking call that stalls everyone, and an edge-triggered descriptor that stalls itself. Those two are the entire discipline of event-driven programming, and having caused both on purpose is what makes them recognisable later.

cheatsheet: A readiness call sleeps until at least one watched descriptor can proceed
The loop is the same regardless of mechanism: wait, then handle each ready descriptor
select: fixed descriptor limit, whole set passed every call, must rescan
poll: no fixed limit, but still passes and rescans the whole array
epoll: registered once, reports only what is ready — cost tracks active, not open
Check FD_SETSIZE on your system; exceeding it is undefined behaviour that may appear to work
Level-triggered reports while data remains; edge-triggered reports only on change
Edge-triggered requires non-blocking descriptors and reading until EAGAIN
Nothing in the loop may block — one slow call stalls every connection

checkpoint.prompt: A server watches 10,000 connections of which 3 are active. Why does epoll outperform poll here?

choices.D: poll passes and examines all 10,000 every call

checkpoint.explanation: Epoll is told the set once and reports only the 3 that are ready. The cost of poll tracks the number of descriptors watched; the cost of epoll tracks the number that became ready. That is a structural difference, not a tuning one.

checkpoint.prompt: Your event loop calls a database query that takes 200 ms. What happens to the other connections?

choices.D: They are served by another thread

checkpoint.explanation: One blocking call stalls the entire loop. One thread means one thing at a time. This is why event-driven runtimes hand slow work to a thread pool instead of performing it inside the loop.

checkpoint.prompt: With edge-triggered epoll, a descriptor is reported readable and you read 100 of the 500 bytes available. What happens next?

choices.A: It is not reported again until new data arrives
choices.D: The kernel buffers it and retries

checkpoint.explanation: The remaining 400 bytes sit unread and that connection stalls. Edge-triggered reports state changes, not state. You must drain the descriptor by reading until EAGAIN, which is why it also requires non-blocking mode.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is select unsuitable for a server that may accumulate thousands of connections?

choices.D: Its descriptor set is a fixed-size structure, and using a descriptor number at or above the limit is undefined behaviour

checkpoint.explanation: The limit is a compile-time constant, and exceeding it writes past the end of a structure — undefined behaviour that may appear to work, which is the most dangerous kind.
